chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, who said:

I asked him about a man who goes to the market and buys a fur cloak, not knowing whether it is from an animal slaughtered according to ritual law or not. Should he pray in it? He said, 'Yes. There is no burden of inquiry upon you. Indeed, Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) used to say, "Indeed, the Khawarij narrowed things upon themselves through their ignorance. Indeed, the religion is broader than that."'

key_terms.الْخَوَارِجَ: The Khawarij (a sect known for strictness and extremism)
key_terms.لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَسْأَلَةُ: There is no burden of inquiry upon you

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray in a fur cloak if I don't know if the animal was ritually slaughtered?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia principle of *al-asl al-istishab* (presumption of continuity) in cases of doubt regarding the ritual slaughter status of animal skins. Imam al-Baqir’s reference to the Khawarij highlights how their excessive rigorism (*ghuluw*) imposed undue hardship, contrasting with the Shia emphasis on ease (*taysir*) and the default permissibility of items unless proven otherwise. This ruling reinforces the broader jurisprudential stance that uncertainty does not invalidate worship, aligning with the Quranic maxim that God intends no difficulty for believers.
